node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Ask counting questions
node.description: Ask simple questions that can be answered by counting responses or objects.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sort data into categories
node.description: Sort responses or objects into clear categories for counting and comparison.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Category labels
node.description: Use clear labels so that each category in a data set has a meaning.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Categorical and numerical data
node.description: Distinguish data that describe categories from data that record numbers or measurements.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Question matches data
node.description: Check whether the data collected can answer the statistical question being asked.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Refine statistical questions
node.description: Improve vague questions so they identify a group, variable and data collection method.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Tally marks
node.description: Use tally marks to record counts efficiently during data collection.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Frequency tables
node.description: Organise counts or measurements in frequency tables for analysis and display.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Survey data collection
node.description: Collect data by asking consistent survey questions to a selected group.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Observation data collection
node.description: Collect data by observing and recording events, behaviours or objects systematically.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Experimental data collection
node.description: Collect data from simple experiments where conditions or trials are controlled.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Data cleaning checks
node.description: Check collected data for missing, duplicated, inconsistent or impossible values.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Population and sample
node.description: Distinguish the population of interest from the sample that provides data.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sample size
node.description: Interpret how sample size affects reliability, variability and confidence in data-based claims.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Random sampling introduction
node.description: Use random selection ideas to reduce selection bias in samples.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Representative samples
node.description: Judge whether a sample reasonably reflects the population for the question being asked.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sampling bias
node.description: Identify ways a sample or collection method may systematically favour some outcomes.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Response bias
node.description: Identify how wording, context or respondent behaviour can bias survey responses.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Ethical data collection
node.description: Consider privacy, consent and fairness when collecting and using data.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Plan a data investigation
node.description: Plan a statistical investigation by connecting question, data source, collection method and analysis plan.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Record measurement data
node.description: Record measurement data with consistent units, precision and labels.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Statistical question expects variability
node.description: A statistical question expects answers that may vary across people, objects or trials.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Categories need clear rules
node.description: Categories should be defined clearly enough that responses can be sorted consistently.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Categorical data are labels
node.description: Categorical data describe groups or qualities rather than measurements on a numerical scale.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Numerical data are counts or measures
node.description: Numerical data record counts or measurements that can be ordered or calculated with.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Frequency is count
node.description: Frequency records how often a category or value occurs.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Population is full group
node.description: The population is the full group that a statistical question or claim is about.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sample represents population
node.description: A sample is useful when it reasonably represents the population for the question being asked.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Random sampling reduces selection bias
node.description: Random selection can reduce systematic bias in who or what is included in a sample.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Bias can distort conclusions
node.description: Bias in sampling, measurement or response can make conclusions misleading.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Data collection needs consistency
node.description: Consistent definitions, units and procedures make data more trustworthy and comparable.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Any question is statistical
node.description: Learner treats any question as statistical even when it has a single fixed answer and no expected variability.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Overlapping categories
node.description: Learner creates categories that overlap or leave responses without a clear place.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sample equals population
node.description: Learner treats the sample as if it were automatically the entire population.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Larger sample always representative
node.description: Learner assumes a larger sample is representative even when the sampling method is biased.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Biased wording treated as neutral
node.description: Learner misses how survey wording can lead respondents toward particular answers.

edge.rationale: Asking countable questions is an early form of statistical questioning.
Sorting into categories is central to categorical data questions.
Category labels make categorical data interpretable.
Distinguishing categorical and numerical data supports matching questions to data types.
A statistical question must match data that can answer it.
Refining questions deepens statistical-question design.
Tally marks are a basic data recording method.
Frequency tables organise collected counts and values.
Surveying is a common data collection method.
Observation is a common data collection method.
Experiments are a more structured data collection method.
Cleaning checks support trustworthy collected data.
Measurement data recording is a common numerical data collection case.
Population and sample are core concepts in sampling.
Sample size affects reliability and variability of sample evidence.
Random sampling is a standard method for reducing selection bias.
Representativeness is central to interpreting sample quality.
Sampling bias is a core risk in sampling and representativeness.
Response bias affects survey-based sampling and conclusions.
Ethical data collection supports responsible sampling and data use.
Planning a data investigation connects question, sampling and collection decisions.
Early counting questions require understanding that counts answer how-many questions.
edge.failure_signal: Learner asks questions but cannot connect responses to counts.

edge.rationale: Sorting responses into categories builds from asking countable questions about attributes.
edge.failure_signal: Learner mixes categories or sorts by unrelated attributes.

edge.rationale: Category labels formalise sorted groups so they can be interpreted later.
edge.failure_signal: Learner sorts objects but cannot name categories clearly.

edge.rationale: Distinguishing data types requires first understanding categorical labels.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats all responses as labels or all responses as numbers regardless of meaning.

edge.rationale: Matching questions to data requires knowing whether the response data are categorical or numerical.
edge.failure_signal: Learner collects data that do not answer the question or uses the wrong data type.

edge.rationale: Refining statistical questions depends on judging whether the data can answer the question.
edge.failure_signal: Learner improves wording superficially without making the question measurable or variable.

edge.rationale: Tally marks record counts for categories or values during collection.
edge.failure_signal: Learner makes marks but does not link them consistently to categories.

edge.rationale: Frequency tables organise counts such as tallies into a table.
edge.failure_signal: Learner records tallies but cannot convert them into category frequencies.

edge.rationale: Surveys require questions that match the intended data and respondents.
edge.failure_signal: Learner writes survey questions that are ambiguous or unrelated to the investigation.

edge.rationale: Observation data collection often records event counts or values systematically.
edge.failure_signal: Learner observes events but does not record them consistently enough for analysis.

edge.rationale: Simple experiments add controlled trials to systematic observation and recording.
edge.failure_signal: Learner changes several conditions at once or records trials inconsistently.

edge.rationale: Recording measurement data depends on using consistent measurement units, though the specific unit type depends on context.
edge.failure_signal: Learner records measurements without consistent units or precision.

edge.rationale: Cleaning checks require organised data so missing or inconsistent values can be detected.
edge.failure_signal: Learner analyses data without noticing missing, duplicate or impossible values.

edge.rationale: Population and sample concepts build on knowing who or what data were collected from.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot say what larger group the collected data are intended to represent.

edge.rationale: Sample size is interpreted relative to the population and the investigation question.
edge.failure_signal: Learner judges reliability only by the existence of a sample, not its size or variability.

edge.rationale: Random sampling requires identifying the population from which the sample is selected.
edge.failure_signal: Learner chooses cases casually and calls the result random.

edge.rationale: Representativeness requires comparing the sample with the population of interest.
edge.failure_signal: Learner assumes a convenient sample represents the whole population.

edge.rationale: Sampling bias is identified by considering whether a sample systematically fails to represent the population.
edge.failure_signal: Learner notices sample size but not who is systematically included or excluded.

edge.rationale: Response bias is most visible when evaluating how survey questions and contexts shape answers.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats leading survey wording as neutral.

edge.rationale: Ethical considerations should shape investigation plans, though they can be introduced earlier as norms.
edge.failure_signal: Learner collects sensitive data without considering privacy, consent or fairness.

edge.rationale: Planning a data investigation should account for sampling method, bias and data quality.
edge.failure_signal: Learner plans a collection method that cannot answer the question reliably.
